query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, friction-induced thermal activation at elevated temperatures forms a heterogeneous, protective oxide layer that spalls due to mechanical mismatches at the phase interfaces. The resulting losses of the protective film expose reactive substrate regions to a corrosive environment while detached oxide fragments act as abrasives, thereby synergistically accelerating both wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA having a ductile matrix coexisting with harder intermetallic/sigma phases that create internal mechanical heterogeneity.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear and corrosive attack at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–800 °C).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (≥600 °C) under cyclic sliding contact in the presence of a corrosive medium (such as a NaCl-containing atmosphere), where both frictional heating and chemical attack are active.
generation.structural_mediator: An in situ–formed, heterogeneous oxide layer that initially protects the surface but undergoes spallation particularly at phase boundaries where local strain mismatches occur.
generation.mechanism: Frictional heating triggers tribo-oxidation, leading to the formation of a protective oxide film. However, due to differential mechanical properties between the eutectic phases (e.g., ductile matrix versus brittle intermetallic phases), stress concentrates at phase interfaces. Under cyclic loading, this stress causes the oxide layer to spall. Once spalled, the fresh substrate becomes rapidly corroded, and the detached oxide debris act as abrasives, cumulatively accelerating material degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline under isolated wear or corrosion, the alloy will display a significantly higher overall degradation. Both the wear rate and the corrosion rate are expected to increase—accelerated wear from abrasive action and loss of lubrication by the spalled oxide layer, and accelerated corrosion from the exposure of vulnerable, unoxidized regions.
generation.baseline: The same alloy subjected to only wear or only corrosion at the same elevated temperature, which should show lower degradation rates and more stable oxide film formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate when the temperature is sufficiently high (≥600 °C) to promote both significant oxide formation and thermal softening, and when the eutectic microstructure exhibits enough phase mechanical mismatch to induce spallation. At lower temperatures or with a more homogeneous microstructure, this mechanism may not be as prominent.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of wear and corrosion to overall degradation remain imprecise, and variability in alloy composition or microstructural control could modulate the spallation behavior and thus the coupling effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the eutectic HEA and split them into three groups: (A) simultaneous wear and corrosion at 600–800 °C, (B) wear only under the same thermal conditions in an inert atmosphere, and (C) corrosion only at the same temperature without mechanical load. Use in situ high-temperature SEM and Raman spectroscopy to monitor oxide layer formation and spallation. Conduct profilometry to measure wear track dimensions and perform electrochemical tests (polarization curves and EIS) to assess corrosion rates.
measurements: Wear track depth, width, and morphology (via SEM/profilometry)
Corrosion current densities and impedance characteristics (electrochemical measurements)
Continuity and spallation events of the oxide layer (in situ high-temperature SEM, Raman spectroscopy)
Phase identification and microstructural evolution (XRD, EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneity of wear and corrosion does not result in significantly higher degradation (i.e., combined wear and corrosion metrics do not exceed the sum or expected synergistic effect of groups B and C), or if no evidence of oxide layer spallation correlates with accelerated substrate corrosion and wear, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. For NiX, its worn track dimensions also increase at 400 °C compared to those at RT, but the worn surface remains relatively smooth and is free of debris and micro-pits (Fig. S7b). This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa). Combined with the SEM results and EDS analysis, it can be seen that the worn surfaces of both CCAs have a low oxygen concentration (<20 at.%) at 400 °C and do not form a visible protective oxide layer, as evidenced by cross-sectional observations of the worn tracks (Fig. S10a and b). Concurrently, the in situ formation of alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides further inhibits the grain coarsening by dissipating frictional energy. Therefore, the cooperative heterostructure in the NiX activates the dense nanocrystalline glaze layer during high-temperature wear, thus minimizing the adhesive and oxidative wear between the tribo-pairs. From the above analyses, the underlying wear mechanisms responsible for the unprecedented wear resistance in the NiX are schematically illustrated in Fig. S23. During sliding at RT, the intrinsic structures of NiX rely on multiple deformation pathways to evoke the NC tribo-layer and the UFG tribo-layer, thus progressively accommodating the gradient elastic–plastic deformation distributed along the friction interface. During sliding at 800 °C, the intrinsic structures of NiX are able to promote the formation of a dense glaze layer and a deformed tribo-layer containing alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides through spontaneous tribochemical reactions, which dramatically suppress adhesive and oxidative wear between tribo-pairs.

Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.
